Real Analysis Lecture 8: Fubini’s Theorem
Oct 26, 2025
  • Real_analysis

Disclaimer: This post is a personal study note based on the Real Analysis course I attended.

(08a) Fubini’s Theorem

Let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb{C}$ and write
[ f_x(y) = f(x,y), \qquad f^y(x) = f(x,y). ]

Tonelli’s Theorem

If $f : (\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{T})$ - measurable and $f \ge 0$, then

  1. For each $x$,
    $f_x : Y \to \lbrack 0,\infty\rbrack$ is $\mathcal{T}$-measurable.

  2. For each $y$,
    $f^y : X \to \lbrack 0,\infty\rbrack$ is $\mathcal{S}$-measurable.

  3. The functions
    [ x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\, d\nu \quad\text{and}\quad
    y \mapsto \int_X f^y\, d\mu ] are $\mathcal{S}$-measurable and $\mathcal{T}$-measurable.

Moreover, [ \int_{X\times Y} f\, d(\mu\times\nu) = \int_X \left( \int_Y f_x \, d\nu \right) d\mu = \int_Y \left( \int_X f^y \, d\mu \right) d\nu. ]

Fubini’s Theorem

If $f \in L^1(\mu\times\nu)$, i.e. [ \int_{X\times Y} \lvert f(x,y)\rvert \, d(\mu\times\nu) < \infty, ] then:

  • $f_x \in L^1(\nu)$ for a.e. $x$
  • $f^y \in L^1(\mu)$ for a.e. $y$

Define [ \varphi(x) = \int_Y f_x\, d\nu(y), \qquad \psi(y) = \int_X f^y\, d\mu(x). ]

Then [ \varphi \in L^1(\mu), \qquad \psi \in L^1(\nu), ] and [ \int_{X\times Y} f\, d(\mu\times\nu) = \int_X \varphi\, d\mu = \int_Y \psi \, d\nu. ]

(08b) Borel Product & Lebesgue Measure

Consider $(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}, m\times m)$.

Let
[ \mathcal{L}_2 = (\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L})^\ast ] be the completion of the product measure.

Definition: Completion of a measure space

For a measure space $(X, \mathcal{A}, \mu)$, the completion is the process of enlarging $\mathcal{A}$ by including all subsets of measure–zero sets. Formally, the completed $\sigma$–algebra is
[ \mathcal{A}^\ast = \lbrace E \subseteq X : \exists A,B \in \mathcal{A},\ A \subseteq E \subseteq B,\ \mu(B \setminus A)=0 \rbrace. ] This makes every null set and every subset of a null set measurable.

We conclude [ \mathcal{B}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L} \subseteq (\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L})^\ast. ]

pf)

1. $\mathcal{B}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}$

  • $\mathcal{B}_2$ is the Borel σ-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^2$, generated by all open sets.
  • Every open set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ belongs to $\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}$ because:
    • open sets in $\mathbb{R}$ are Lebesgue measurable,
    • products of Lebesgue measurable sets are measurable in $\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}$,
    • $\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}$ is a σ-algebra and contains all measurable rectangles.
  • Since $\mathcal{B}_2$ is the smallest σ-algebra containing all open sets,
    it must be contained in any σ-algebra that contains all open sets.

2. $\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L} \subseteq (\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L})^\ast$

  • $(\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L})^\ast$ is the completion of the product σ-algebra.
  • By definition of completion, [ \mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{A}^\ast \qquad\text{for any σ-algebra } \mathcal{A}. ]
  • Thus every set in the Lebesgue product σ-algebra automatically belongs to its completion.

Theorem 8-3.

If $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ is $\mathcal{L}$-measurable, then

$\exists\; g: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ Borel–measurable with $f=g\;$ a.e.

pf)

Let $f = \sum_{k=1}^\infty c_k \cdot \chi_{E_k}$.

Take $g = \sum_{k=1}^\infty c_k \cdot \chi_{A_k}$ s.t.

  • $A_k, B_k$ Borel-measurable,
  • $A_k \subseteq E \subseteq B_k$,
  • $(m \times m)^\ast(B_k\setminus A_k)=0$.

Property 8-1.

If $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ is $\mathcal{L}$-measurable, then

[ \Rightarrow f = g + h ] , wherer $g$ is Borel-measurable and $h$ is zero a.e.

(08c) Convolution of Integrable Functions

Let $f,g \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

Definition: Convolution

For $f, g \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, [ (f\ast g)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)\, g(x-y)\, dy. ]

This corresponds to the “real” version of the group algebra convolution.

Basic Computation

Using Fubini’s Theorem and translation invariance of Lebesgue measure:

[ \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left\lbrace \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert f(y)g(x-y) \rvert \, dx \right\rbrace dy \le \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left\lbrace \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert f(y)\rvert \; \lvert g(x-y) \rvert \, dx \right\rbrace dy ] [ = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left\lbrace \lvert f(y) \rvert \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert g(x-y) \rvert \, dx \right\rbrace dy ] [ = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left\lbrace \lvert f(y) \rvert \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert g(x) \rvert \, dx \right\rbrace dy ] [ = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert f(y) \rvert \, dy \cdot \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert g(x) \rvert \, dx ]

Thus, [ \lVert f\ast g \rVert_1 \le \lVert f\rVert_1 \lVert g\rVert_1. ]

This shows that $(L^1(\mathbb{R}), \ast)$ is a Banach algebra.

Definition: Banach Algebra

A Banach algebra is a mathematical structure that combines:

  1. Banach space
    A complete normed vector space (every Cauchy sequence converges).

  2. Algebra structure
    A multiplication operation $a \ast b$ defined on the space that is associative and bilinear.

  3. Norm compatibility
    The multiplication satisfies [ \lVert a \ast b \rVert \le \lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert. ]

Algebraic Properties

For $f,g,h\in L^1$:

  1. $(f\ast g)\ast h = f\ast(g\ast h)$
  2. $(af + bg)\ast h = af\ast h + bg\ast h$
  3. $f\ast g = g\ast f$
  4. $(f\ast g)’ = f\ast g’$

Approximation via Convolution

Let $1<p,q<\infty$ and $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1$.

If $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R})$ and $g\in L^q(\mathbb{R})$, then [ f\ast g \in L^\infty. ]

pf)

Hölder’s inequality gives: [ \lvert(f\ast g)(x)\rvert = \left\lvert\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y) g(x-y)\, dy\right\rvert = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lvert f(y) g_{-x}(-y) \rvert \, dy \le \lVert f\rVert_p \lVert g\rVert_q. ]

Theorem 8-4.

If $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R})$ and $g\in L^q(\mathbb{R})$, then
[ f\ast g \in C_0(\mathbb{R}). ]

pf)

Let $x_n\to x$. Then [ (f\ast g)(x_n) - (f\ast g)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)g(x_n-y)\, dy - \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)g(x-y)\, dy. ]

Rewrite: [ (f\ast g)(x_n)-(f\ast g)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y) \lbrack g(x_n-y)-g(x-y) \rbrack \, dy. ]

Let $h_n := x_n - x$, [ (f \ast g)(x_n) - (f \ast g)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)\, \lbrack g(x + h_n - y) - g(x - y) \rbrack \, dy ] [ = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x - t)\, \lbrack g(t + h_n) - g(t) \rbrack \, dt. ]

Let $\tau_{h} g(t) = g(t + h)$ and using Hölder’s inequality, [ \lvert (f \ast g)(x_n) - (f \ast g)(x) \rvert \le \lVert f \rVert_p \, \lVert \tau_{h_n} g - g \rVert_q. ]

By the previously established result on the $L^{q}$–continuity of translations, [ h_n \to 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lVert \tau_{h_n} g - g \rVert_q \to 0. ]

Consequently, [ (f \ast g)(x_n) \to (f \ast g)(x), ] which shows that $f \ast g$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

📚 Reference: Real Analysis Lecture by Prof. Seung-Hyeok Kye (SNU)
